title: Global Water Footprint Assessment
summary: The Global Water Footprint Assessment research program quantifies the water resources used to support food production and consumption and examines how these patterns change across space and time. The program includes long-term assessment of global crop water footprints, initially covering 1972–2018, and has expanded to global livestock production, national water footprints of consumption, and international virtual water flows for 1972–2023. Together, these efforts provide a consistent framework for understanding historical changes in water use and the connections among production, consumption, and global trade.

title: Global Hydrological Modeling & Water Scarcity Assessment
summary: The Global Hydrological Modeling & Water Scarcity Assessment project examines the spatial and temporal variability of freshwater availability and water scarcity at large scales. The research combines hydrological modeling with water-use information to assess how the balance between water availability and human demand varies across locations and over time. The work supports improved characterization of water scarcity and provides a hydrologic foundation for evaluating pressures on freshwater resources and broader water-security challenges.

title: PFAS Footprint & Water-Quality Risk Assessment
funding: National Science Foundation, OIA RII Track-2, Award #2019561
summary: This project examines the sources, environmental pathways, and groundwater risks of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The research develops spatially explicit inventories of PFAS releases from diffuse consumer-product pathways and investigates PFAS fate and transport in soils and groundwater using modeling, machine learning, and laboratory experiments. The work also evaluates PFAS sorption behavior and enhanced adsorbent materials for contaminant removal. Together, these efforts connect PFAS sources, environmental processes, groundwater risk, and remediation to support more resilient water-quality management.

title: Drought Impacts and Water Management in the Upper Colorado River Basin
summary: This collaborative project examined how extreme drought affects agricultural and urban communities and environmental systems in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Our research focused on quantifying the economic and environmental impacts of drought under existing water-management practices and the prior-appropriation system. The broader project investigated how coordinated reservoir operations and water-market strategies could reduce drought impacts and strengthen community resilience under changing climate extremes.

title: Mapping and Predicting Water Use by Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations
summary: This project developed a scalable approach for mapping Concentrated Animal Feeding Operations (CAFOs) and estimating their water consumption and withdrawals at high spatial and temporal resolution. By integrating remote sensing data and machine learning, the research addresses critical data gaps in the location, size, and water demands of livestock operations. The resulting information supports improved livestock water-use estimation and provides spatial data relevant to water-resource planning and environmental management.

title: Improving Streamflow Predictions by Incorporating Water Withdrawals
summary: This project investigates how surface-water and groundwater withdrawals affect streamflow prediction, particularly during non-peak and low-flow conditions. The research compiles and characterizes water withdrawals and their sources, including surface-water bodies and groundwater aquifer systems, and evaluates where and to what extent incorporating these human water uses into hydrologic models improves streamflow prediction. The work focuses on the Mississippi Embayment, where groundwater and surface-water withdrawals are important components of the regional water balance.

title: Standard and Impact-Based Low-Flow and Hydrologic Drought Thresholds
summary: This project is developing nationally consistent, observation-based thresholds for characterizing low-flow and hydrologic drought conditions across the United States. The research aims to strengthen drought monitoring, forecasting, and communication by developing standardized thresholds, evaluating forecast reliability, and linking hydrologic conditions with meaningful drought impacts. The project will provide operational guidance and reusable workflows to support more consistent and actionable low-flow and drought information.
